label: PROLOGUE
title: A World beneath Eternal Twilight
p: The lecture hall was filled with the low hum of students chatting and rustling papers. As the lights dimmed, all eyes turned to the front where Prof. Malick stood, his sharp eyes scanning the room. He adjusted his glasses and tapped a piece of chalk against the board, where he had written:
“The Science of Hidden Dimensions and Alternate Realities.”
The students fell silent, curiosity aroused by the mysterious title. Prof. Malick began with a measured tone, his voice calm yet carrying an undercurrent of excitement.

“What if I told you the universe was more than what you see? That right beside you, another world might be watching?” he said, letting the question linger. “Today, we venture into the realm where science meets the extraordinary. We’re going to explore a concept that, at first glance, may sound like pure fiction, the idea of hidden dimensions existing alongside our own. But as the great physicist Dr. Michio Kaku once said, ‘What we usually consider impossible is simply a matter of figuring out how it works.’”
He paused, letting the students absorb his words.

“For most of human history, we believed the world was flat. Then, we discovered it was round. Now, we know it exists in a vast universe with galaxies beyond counting. But what if I told you that there are dimensions beyond the ones we see, the hidden worlds existing right alongside ours?”
Prof. Malick turned to the board and drew a simple diagram, showing three familiar axes “X, Y, and Z”, representing the three dimensions of space.

“The universe as we understand it, exists in four dimensions, three of space and one of time. However, according to String Theory, proposed by scientists like Leonard Susskind and Edward Witten, there may be additional dimensions that are hidden from our perception. These extra dimensions could be folded up like tiny scrolls, existing on a microscopic scale that we cannot see.”
The students leaned in, their interest growing.

“To truly understand this, we need to consider the work of physicists like Theodor Kaluza and Oskar Klein, who, in the early 20th century, suggested that adding a fifth dimension could unify gravity with electromagnetism. Kaluza and Klein were among the first to suggest that these hidden dimensions could be compactified, so small and tightly curled that they are nearly impossible to detect.”
Prof. Malick’s voice took on a more passionate tone, his hands gesturing as he spoke.

“But why stop there?” he asked, eyes gleaming. “Physicists like Lisa Randall and Raman Sundrum have proposed that our universe could be like a membrane, or ‘brane,’ floating in a higher-dimensional space. In other words, there may be entire worlds whole dimensions just a hair’s breadth away from us, yet completely invisible.”
Prof. Malick paused, letting the room breathe before continuing in a softer tone.
“But what if, somewhere beyond our understanding, these dimensions could be accessed? Imagine a place where the history we know took a different path. Imagine... an Africa that was never colonized.”
The students exchanged curious glances as Prof. Malick moved to a new section of the board, erasing the scientific diagrams and drawing a simple map of the African continent.

“You see,” he said, “the idea of alternate realities is not just confined to physics. What if one of these dimensions harbored a world where Africa’s great empires like the Mali Empire of Mansa Musa and the powerful kingdoms of Great Zimbabwe and Benin continued to flourish, untouched by the shadow of colonialism? A world where the scramble for Africa never happened and the continent evolved on its terms.”
He turned to the class, eyes alight with intensity.

“Mystics, philosophers, and spiritual thinkers like Pythagoras, Hermes Trismegistus, and Rudolf Steiner have all spoken of other dimensions. In one such dimension, Africa emerges as a beacon of scientific knowledge, philosophy, and technological innovation. Great cities like Timbuktu, Kano, and Kilwa flourish as centers of learning, their libraries rivaling the ancient wonders of Alexandria. United under a shared purpose, the empires of this world advance technologies that even we have yet to discover.”

A student raised her hand, her brow furrowed. “But Professor, if this alternate Africa is so advanced, how did they achieve such unity? Surely, history teaches us that power always leads to conflict.”

Prof. Malick nodded, acknowledging her point with a thoughtful expression. “You are correct,” he said. “And that is where legend intertwines with reality. There is this one dimension, it is said that a powerful artifact, a ring known as the Simbarashe played a key role in uniting the kingdoms, the word Simbarashe means ‘the power of God.’”

“This, in our world, would have been known as King Solomon’s ring, believed to control spirits and celestial beings. In that alternate dimension, the Simbarashe ring was passed down through generations, inherited by rulers who wielded it to maintain peace and power.”

“This ring was believed to grant its bearer incredible powers, control over the forces of nature, the ability to heal and influence over the hearts of men but the ring did not serve just anyone,” Prof. Malick continued. “It was said to choose its bearer only those of true divine lineage were deemed worthy.”

The room dimmed as Prof. Malick lowered the lights, projecting an image onto the screen. A regal figure stood tall atop a windswept mountain, the Simbarashe ring glowing on his finger. The power it radiated was almost tangible, as though it could reach through time itself.
Prof. Malick paused, his gaze lingering on the image.

“What happened to the ring in our world is a mystery. Some believe it was lost forever. Others claim it is waiting to choose again but in another time, another world, the Simbarashe ring was not lost”

label: CHAPTER 1
title: The Star of Destiny
p: The harbor of Mji Mkuu, the capital city of the Great Swahili Nation, thrummed with energy as the royal fleet approached. The sun hung high, casting golden light over the rippling waters. Banners adorned with the royal crest of a bird cradling the sun fluttered atop ships, their masts towering like sentinels. The rhythmic beat of drums echoed over the waves, a ceremonial welcome for King Jabulani’s return.
On the pier, citizens from every corner of the nation gathered. Women in colorful kitenge wraps waved their scarves, while men in tailored kanzu and hats stood with arms crossed in pride.

Children darted between the crowds, laughing and chasing one another, their joy infectious. Merchants lined the docks with stalls selling fried cassava, spiced fish skewers, and honey-dipped fritters. The air was alive with the mingling aromas of food, sea salt, and anticipation.

The ships docked in unison, their crews expertly securing them with thick ropes. From the tallest ship, King Jabulani stood at the prow, his figure commanding yet shadowed by unease. His deep blue silk robes embroidered with golden threads rippled in the breeze. The Simbarashe ring, a band of intricate carvings said to channel divine power, weighed heavily on his finger.
Though his posture remained majestic, his heart was burdened by the challenges of his recent journey.

"What kind of world will my son inherit if I fail to protect these waters?" Jabulani murmured to Minister Tawanda, his closest advisor. "China seeks partnership, yet their eyes linger on domination. And the West tightens its grip on the seas. Our waters are no longer our own."
"Then we must strengthen our fleets, Your Majesty, " Tawanda replied, his voice steady despite the storm brewing in his mind. "Trade is our lifeblood, but vigilance will be our shield."

Jabulani nodded, though doubt lingered in his eyes. Beyond the shores of Alkebulan, the world was changing. Nations once held at bay now encroached with treaties that reeked of subjugation. The king’s thoughts drifted to his newborn son. His arrival marked a new era, a divine sign of hope but also a reminder of the immense responsibility Jabulani bore.

As the ship docked, the crowd erupted in cheers. Drummers increased their tempo, and women tossed petals of roses into the air. Soldiers of the royal guard stood at attention, their armor polished to a mirror-like sheen. Jabulani raised his hand, silencing the noise momentarily before his rich, resonant voice carried over the masses.
"People of the Great Swahili Nation! Your king returns with wisdom to fortify our land and the grace of the heavens to bless us all. Today, we unite not in fear but in strength."

The crowd roared, their spirits lifted by his words. Yet as Jabulani descended the gangplank, his gaze remained fixed on the towering palace in the distance, its golden domes gleaming under the midday sun.

Inside the palace of Mji Mkuu, the scent of freshly prepared feasts wafted through the great halls. Platters laden with spiced pilau, roasted goat, and fresh seafood were carried by servants in vibrant attire. Bowls of tropical fruits like mangoes, papayas, and golden pineapples glistened like jewels under the glow of ornate lanterns. Large jugs of honeyed wine and freshly brewed hibiscus tea sat ready to quench the thirst of honored guests.

The Great Hall itself was a marvel. Its walls, carved from ivory stone, were adorned with intricate murals depicting the victories of past kings. At its center stood a grand table, draped in silks of emerald and gold, where Queen Makila awaited her husband’s return. Despite her serene expression, her heart was heavy. Only three days had passed since she had given birth to their firstborn son, and exhaustion still clung to her.

Makila’s mind raced with conflicting emotions. The joy of her son’s birth was tempered by the fear of what lay ahead. She had overheard whispers among the ministers about growing threats from foreign powers seeking footholds in their waters, and murmurs of discontent among the provinces. But her greatest fear was for her son. The divine star that shone above Mji Mkuu marked him as special but it also painted a target on his tiny chest.

In her arms lay a new born, swaddled in soft linens, his tiny face glowing as if kissed by the heavens. His presence filled the room with inexplicable warmth, a light that seemed to emanate from his very being.
When the doors opened and Jabulani entered, Makila’s lips curved into a weary but genuine smile. "My king, " she greeted softly.
Jabulani hurried to her side, his strong hands cradling her shoulders. "You shouldn’t have risen, Makila. You’re still recovering."
"How could I remain seated when you have returned to me?" she replied, lifting the swaddled child toward him.
The king’s breath caught as he gazed at his son. His tiny fists clenched as though prepared for battle, his features serene yet commanding. Jabulani’s voice trembled with reverence. "His name?"
"I waited for you, " Makila said. "The shamans are coming."

As if summoned by her words, a distant hum grew louder. Through the palace windows, the courtyards filled with cloaked figures and shamans from every corner of Alkebulan. Their staffs struck the earth in rhythm as they chanted, a melody that carried ancient power. The ministers and soldiers watched in awe as the procession moved toward the great hall.

One shaman, an elder with silver hair and skin etched with sacred markings, stepped forward. He placed his staff beside the child and spoke in a voice that reverberated through the hall. "This child bears the mark of destiny. The heavens have spoken. His name shall be Akachi...the Hand of God."

The room erupted in celebration. Ministers knelt before the child, soldiers saluted and women sang praises. But Jabulani, his joy tempered by a strange unease, held his son aloft for all to see. "My son, my king, my Alkebulan’s light."

The banquet began with great fanfare. Musicians played melodies on traditional stringed instruments, their music weaving through the hall like threads of gold. Dancers dressed in pink garments twirled across the marble floor, their movements fluid and mesmerizing. The air was thick with the aroma of roasted meats and sweet spices.

Yet amidst the revelry, a shadow lingered. A maid approached the king with a goblet of wine. Her hands trembled slightly as she placed it before him. Jabulani, lost in a moment of joy, raised the goblet to his lips and drank deeply.

Time slowed. The music dimmed. Jabulani’s hand froze midair, his body stiffening. The goblet slipped from his grasp, shattering on the floor with a sound like thunder. The hall fell silent as all eyes turned to the king.
"Jabulani?" Makila’s voice cracked with fear.
The king clutched his chest, gasping for breath. "love, " he choked out, his voice a hoarse whisper.

Guards rushed forward as panic erupted. Ministers shouted in confusion, nobles fled their seats, and Queen Makila cradled Akachi protectively. Mateso remained seated, his expression one of carefully constructed shock. He rose slowly, his voice calm yet commanding. "The King is poisoned.
Seal the palace, Find the culprit!"
The king’s body slumped to the floor. His breathing slowed, his gaze fixed on Akachi in Makila’s arms. His lips parted as if to speak, but no words came. His eyes drifted shut.

"Jabulani!" Makila’s anguished cry pierced the air. The investigation into the king’s death revealed chilling truths. The poison, a substance unlike anything seen in Alkebulan was traced to foreign origins. A small vial found in the maid’s quarters pointed to her involvement but before she could confess, she was found dead in her cell. Her neck had been snapped and no trace of an intruder was found.
Fear gripped the palace. Rumors spread of curses and treachery of foreign powers seeking to unravel Alkebulan’s unity. Ministers convened in secrecy but suspicion hung heavy over every decision.

Meanwhile, Mateso moved with calculated precision. The elder prince, long overshadowed by his younger brother, harbored a lifetime of resentment. He despised the shamans who had foretold Jabulani’s rise and scorned the ministers who upheld their prophecies. Now, with the throne within his grasp, he made his move.

The night following the king’s death, Mateso summoned the ministers to the throne room. The air was heavy with tension as he addressed them, his voice cold and unyielding. "My brother’s death is a tragedy, but the kingdom cannot remain leaderless. As the eldest son, the throne is mine by birthright."

A murmur spread through the room, some ministers nodding in reluctant agreement while others exchanged wary glances. Elder Wekesa, the most revered shaman, said firmly. "The throne belongs to Akachi, "He bears the star of destiny, the will of the heavens."
Mateso’s jaw tightened, his dark eyes narrowing. "Enough of this superstition, " he snapped. "The kingdom needs a king, not a child."

label: CHAPTER 2
title: Embers beneath the Throne
p: The throne room was filled with a chill, a cold that seeped into the bones and held the air in a vice-like grip. Golden braziers flickered weakly against the stone walls, their flames barely holding back the darkness. The intricate carvings of ancient kings, those who had once worn the sacred Simbarashe ring and ruled with honor glowed faintly under the dim light. Their carved eyes full of wisdom seemed to silently judge the man who now stood at the center of the room, Mateso.

He stood tall in his dark robes, his presence looming like an eclipse. His eyes, dark and unreadable, scanned the room of ministers and shamans. The tension in the air was palpable, thick with resentment and fear. He had come to claim his birthright but the bitter sting of years spent in the shadows of his brother King Jabulani, still twisted his insides. His fists clenched at his sides, the skin of his knuckles pale, taut with barely suppressed rage.

“Do you cower before me?” Mateso’s voice sliced through the silence, cold and commanding. His words were laced with venom that set the ministers and shamans on edge. “I am the eldest son of our father. The blood of kings flows in my veins. Yet you have defied me for years!”

The braziers hissed, as if protesting his words. A heavy stillness settled over the room, broken only by the faint, rhythmic thud of Elder Wekesa’s staff as he stepped forward. The ancient shaman’s movements were deliberate, his gaze unwavering. Lines of wisdom etched his face and his voice, though soft, carried the weight of countless years.
“You were not chosen, Mateso,” Wekesa said, his tone steady. “Your father did not reject you, the stars did.”

Mateso’s body stiffened as the words hit him like a slap. For a moment, his rage flickered with doubt, pain, even fear. He turned his gaze to the far wall where the grand carving of King Jabulani stood, eternally watching. The king’s likeness, carved in gleaming marble seemed to mock him. It was the image of a king blessed by the heavens and chosen by destiny with the weight of Alkebulan upon his shoulders.
“Since I was a boy, I watched you kneel to my brother,” Mateso muttered, his voice dropping to a venomous growl. “You never saw me, you never believed in me but you always believed in him.”

His fists clenched tighter, his knuckles bone-white. The memories surged forward unbidden, the whispers of his brother’s greatness, the endless accolades and the dismissive glances cast his way. He had been born first yet destiny had robbed him of everything. His sneer twisted into something uglier, a mask of bitterness.
“Now, you will kneel or you will burn.”

The words hung in the air like a curse. The silence that followed was suffocating, crackling with the energy of a coming storm. The ministers and shamans exchanged uneasy glances, their fear was crystal clear yet none dared to speak, none dared to defy the man who now stood before them.

Elder Wekesa held his ground, his gaze unwavering. He took another step forward, his staff striking the marble floor with a sharp crack. The sound echoed through the room, breaking the suffocating silence.
“A king chosen by rage will never know peace, Mateso,” the elder said softly, his voice carrying a warning that seemed to reverberate through the hall. “Your crown will curse this land.”
“Then let the heavens weep!” Mateso roared, his voice rising to a crescendo. His chest heaved with rage, his breathing ragged. The room seemed to vibrate with the intensity of his anger. “Guards!”

The faint metallic scent of armor wafted into the throne room as the doors crashed open with a deafening sound. Soldiers clad in black armor poured into the hall, their swords gleaming under the flickering light of the braziers. The tension in the room snapped like a taut rope, and the ministers and shamans recoiled, fear etched onto their faces.

Mateso turned his back to the room, his gaze fixated on the carving of King Jabulani. The stone king’s serene expression only fueled his rage. His hands clenched into fists once more as he spoke, his words dripping with venom.
“You will no longer haunt me,” he muttered, though it was unclear whether he spoke to the carving or to the memory of his brother.

The soldiers advanced in perfect formation, their boots striking the floor with precision. They formed a wall of steel, their blades pointed toward the shamans and ministers who now stood cornered, their faces pale with fear. The braziers flickered wildly as if the flames themselves sought to escape the growing darkness.
Elder Wekesa remained steadfast. Even as the soldiers stepped closer, even as their swords gleamed with deadly intent, he did not falter. His voice rose above the growing chaos, clear and unyielding.
“The heavens do not weep for tyrants, Mateso,” he said, his tone filled with quiet defiance. “They rain fire to cleanse the land.”

Mateso turned to face the elder, his expression unreadable. For a moment, the room seemed to hold its breath, the tension so thick it felt as if the walls themselves might crack under its weight. Slowly, a sneer spread across his face.
“Kneel,” he said, his voice cold and final, “or share my brother’s fate.”

The ministers hesitated, their fear paralyzing them. One by one, they began to lower themselves to the floor, their gazes cast downward. Yet Elder Wekesa remained standing, his eyes locked onto Mateso’s. His silence was louder than any words, his defiance unbroken.
Mateso took a step closer, his dark robes swirling around him like shadows. His lip curled in disdain as he addressed the elder.
“You may stand, old man but it will not save you,” he said. “Your time has passed. This kingdom is mine now

The throne room was plunged into silence, the weight of impending conflict hanging heavy in the air. In the royal chambers, Queen Makila cradled her newborn son, Akachi in her arms. Her heart ached with the weight of the moment, the future of Alkebulan hanging in the balance. The child’s tiny chest rose and fell in gentle rhythm, unaware of the storm that had begun to sweep across the kingdom. The sound of the baby’s soft cries filled the silence but the queen’s tears, though silent, were endless.

She rocked him slowly, her hands trembling. Each lullaby whispered was a prayer to the heavens, asking for mercy, for guidance and for strength but as much as she wished to shield him, she knew the coming storm would not spare her son. She had seen the signs and had felt the tremor in the earth, the dark tide that had begun to rise.

The door creaked open and Kafele, the leader of the royal guard stepped into the room, his face grim. Behind him, Elder Wekesa and a group of loyalists, shamans, ministers and warriors filed into the room. The lines on their faces were drawn with grief but also with an iron determination.
“Your Majesty,” Kafele said, bowing deeply. “Mateso has begun the slaughter. We have little time.”

Queen Makila’s breath caught in her throat but her voice remained steady. “He cannot find my son,” she whispered fiercely, her arms tightening around Akachi as though to protect him from the fate that threatened. “If he takes Akachi, Alkebulan will be lost. The star will fade, and the land will wither.”
Elder Wekesa stepped forward, placing a hand gently on her shoulder. “The boy carries the star of the first king,” he said softly. “His destiny cannot end here. The heavens will guide him.”

Makila’s face paled but there was a fire in her eyes. She rose to her feet, still clutching Akachi to her chest, her body a fragile shield. “Take him far from here. Shida,” she called to her loyal maid, stepping from the shadows, “you will go with my son.”

Shida, her face streaked with silent tears, stepped forward. Her hands trembled but her resolve was iron. She reached for Akachi, her arms cradling the baby close to her heart. “I will protect him with my life, my queen.”
Makila's eyes met Kafele’s. “You must ensure their escape,” she said. “And you must return for revenge.”
The room fell into silence, the weight of her words pressing heavily upon them all. Kafele nodded sharply, his gaze unwavering. “With my sword, my queen.”
Just then, a faint rustling came from the corridor outside. Everyone froze. Kafele’s hand shot to the hilt of his blade, his eyes narrowing.
“We are discovered,” he whispered, his voice low but filled with command.

Makila’s grip tightened on Akachi as a flicker of resolve hardened her expression. She whispered one last prayer, her lips moving in silence while her heart prepared for the fight ahead. The once-proud halls of the palace were unrecognizable. Blood streaked the marble floors and the bodies of shamans lay crumpled beneath the shattered remnants of their altars. The air itself seemed to mourn, heavy with the metallic stench of death and the smoke of extinguished incense. Shadows, cast by flickering flames, twisted and writhed across the walls like vengeful spirits watching the carnage unfold.

Elder Wekesa fled through hidden passages, his breath ragged as he clutched his staff. This was no longer the palace he had served sanctuary of wisdom and peace. It had become a tomb, filled with the screams of those he once called kin. Yet he ran, clutching his staff, clinging to the fragile hope that the boy could yet survive.
“The boy must live,” Wekesa whispered to himself, his voice barely audible above the chaos. “The star must survive.”

Behind him, the sound of boots grew louder and closer. The guards' heavy steps echoed like a drumbeat of death, each thud pounding in his ears. He could feel the heat of pursuit closing in, every corner of the labyrinthine palace growing smaller and more dangerous. Yet he pushed forward, praying that somewhere in the distance Akachi could still be saved.

Mateso strode through the carnage with calm precision, his dark eyes scanning the bloodsoaked marble floor. To him, this was not destruction but it was rebirth. He moved like a king surveying his kingdom, the cries of the dying fading into nothingness beneath the weight of his ambition. He stopped before a young shaman, his face pale but his spirit unbroken.

The shaman’s robes were torn, blood pooling beneath him, yet his eyes burned with defiance. He raised his chin, trembling but resolute. “You will never find him,” the young shaman rasped, his voice steady despite the agony etched into his features. “The heavens have chosen, and their will cannot be undone.”

Mateso studied him for a moment, the faintest flicker of amusement crossing his face. He crouched to meet the shaman’s gaze, his voice low and edged with cruelty. “The heavens are silent in the face of strength,” he said. “And their stars will burn with the rest of this land.”
The young shaman spat at his feet, a final act of defiance. Mateso straightened, his sneer returning as he motioned to his guards. “Finish him.”

The sword rose and fell, its arc clean and swift. The sound of steel meeting flesh echoed through the chamber followed by the sickening thud of a body collapsing to the floor. The guards stepped back, their faces expressionless while Mateso’s gaze lingered on the growing pool of blood.
“Bring me Wekesa,” he commanded, his tone calm but seething with authority. “And seal the exits. The boy will not leave these walls alive.”

The shadows of the palace deepened, the silence now broken only by the sound of boots pounding marble and the faint cries that still lingered in the distant halls. Mateso walked on, his steps steady and deliberate. This was not chaos to him, it was the forging of order. The future of Alkebulan would be his and no star, no prophecy, would stand in his way. In the throne room, Queen Makila awaited her fate. She stood before her husband’s empty seat, the symbol of a kingdom now lost to the winds of destiny. Her emerald gown shimmered as she stood tall, her face regal even in the face of impending doom. The weight of the crown was gone yet she carried a heavier burden, the future of Alkebulan.

The throne room, once a beacon of majesty felt like a tomb. The faint scent of blood lingered in the air mingling with the acrid smoke from torches that flickered in their sconces. Shadows danced on the walls twisting and mocking the solemnity of the moment.

Mateso entered, his steps slow and deliberate, the sound of his boots echoing against the marble floor. Behind him, his soldiers moved in a precise formation, fanning out to encircle the queen. His dark eyes swept the room before settling on Makila. His lips curled into a sneer as he regarded her.
“Where is the boy?” Mateso’s voice was cold, almost detached, but his words carried the venom of a serpent. “Tell me, and perhaps I will make this swift.”
Makila lifted her chin, her eyes blazing with defiance. “You will never find him,” she said firmly, her voice as steady as the mountains. “He is beyond your reach.”

Mateso’s sneer twisted into a grimace, his fury barely contained. He stepped closer, the shadows swallowing his figure. “You think defiance will save him? You think that your faith will protect him?” His tone dropped to a venomous whisper. “You are alone, Makila.”
Makila’s lips curved into a faint, sorrowful smile. “I am never alone,” she said softly. “God sees me. And He sees you.”
The words struck like a whip, and for a fleeting moment, Mateso’s composure faltered. He quickly masked his unease with a cruel laugh, gesturing sharply to his guards. “Take her.”

The guards approached, their steps hesitant despite the command. Even in her vulnerability, Makila’s presence was unshaken, her aura one of quiet strength. They seized her arms, forcing her to her knees, but she did not resist. She looked up at Mateso, her gaze piercing through his facade.

“You may kill me, Mateso but the soul of this land will never bow to you.”” she said, her voice rising with unyielding conviction. “you might rule this land but its soul will resist you and my people will rise like a morning sun watching you fall.”
Her words hung in the air, heavy and unyielding. The guards hesitated, their grips tightening as they glanced at one another. The queen, even on her knees, seemed to tower over them all.
Mateso’s jaw clenched, his patience worn thin. “Silence her,” he hissed, his voice trembling with suppressed rage.

The guards’ blades gleamed as they drew them, the torches casting ominous reflections on the polished steel. The air grew still as if the room itself held its breath. Makila closed her eyes, her lips moving in a silent prayer. Her heart beat steadily, each pulse a reminder of the child she had protected.

When the blade fell, the wind outside howled, rushing through the shattered windows as if to carry her spirit to the heavens. The torches flickered violently, their light dimming for a heartbeat before returning. The room was silent, except for the faint rustle of fabric as her body crumpled to the floor.

Mateso stood motionless, his gaze fixed on the lifeless form of the queen. The silence that followed was deafening, a void that even his triumph could not fill. For a moment, he felt the weight of her words like a shadow that refused to leave.
The soldiers exchanged uneasy glances, their leader’s stillness unsettling. Finally, Mateso turned, his voice cold and sharp. “Burn her body. Let her name be forgotten.”

But as the flames consumed the queen, the wind carried her final words, a curse that would haunt the throne “The soul of this land will never bow to you.” Nightfall shrouded the forest surrounding the palace, its towering trees casting long shadows beneath the pale glow of the moon. The air was heavy with the hum of distant danger, a tension that gripped the heart and refused to let go.

Shida rode swiftly through the dense woods, her hands gripping the reins with white-knuckled desperation. The thunder of hooves beneath her and the distant cries of pursuit spurred her onward. Akachi’s soft cries were muffled against her chest, his tiny body bundled tightly in her arms. She whispered soothing words to him, her voice trembling. “Hush, my king. We will be safe soon.”

The trees blurred past, their dark forms like silent sentinels bearing witness to her flight. The path twisted and turned, narrowing as she pushed the horse to its limits. Every rustle of leaves, every snap of a twig, sent a shiver of fear down her spine. The enemy was close, their torches a faint, flickering glow in the distance.

“Faster,” she urged the horse, her voice barely a whisper against the pounding rhythm of hooves. Her breath came in sharp bursts, each inhale laced with desperation. The forest opened suddenly, revealing the edge of a cliff. Shida pulled the reins sharply, the horse rearing back with a startled whinny. Below, the cliff dropped into a sea of mist, the rocky base obscured by the swirling vapor. Behind her, the sounds of pursuit grew louder. The rustling of leaves gave way to the clamor of armored boots and torchlight painted the forest in angry hues of orange and red. Shida turned, her heart hammering as the captain of the pursuing soldiers emerged from the shadows. His smirk was cruel, his sword glinting in the firelight.
“There’s nowhere to run,” he said, his voice dripping with malice. “Hand over the child, and I may yet spare your life.”

Shida clutched Akachi tighter, her lips moving in a silent prayer. “For the king,” she whispered, her gaze darting toward the mist below. She would rather leap into the unknown than surrender the future of Alkebulan.

Before the soldiers could advance, a sharp whistle pierced the air. The captain froze, his expression shifting to one of confusion. Then, without warning, arrows rained down from the shadows, striking the soldiers with deadly precision. One by one, they fell, their cries cut short as they crumpled to the forest floor.

Shida’s breath caught as figures emerged from the mist, cloaked in shadows and moving with lethal grace. At their head was Kafele, his sword glinting faintly in the moonlight. His eyes met hers and a flicker of relief crossed his face.
“Come!” he shouted, his voice urgent. He reached for her, his strong hand steadying her trembling form as she dismounted. Shida handed Akachi to him, her heart swelling with gratitude and hope.
The remaining soldiers hesitated, their courage faltering in the face of the Makua warriors who now surrounded them. Kafele turned, his voice a low growl. “Finish them.”

The warriors moved swiftly, their blades gleaming as they descended upon the enemy. Shida followed Kafele into the mist, her steps quick but careful as she clung to the hope that they would escape this nightmare. Akachi’s soft coos reached her ears, a fragile reminder of what they fought to protect.
As they vanished into the shadows, the sounds of battle faded behind them. The forest seemed to close around their path, its towering trees a silent shield against the chaos they left behind.

The palace was a place of hollow triumph. Foreign banners now hung alongside the crests of the Great Swahili Nation, their vibrant colors a stark reminder of the kingdom’s fall. The ornate walls, once symbols of unity and strength, now seemed weighed down by the burden of betrayal. This was not a celebration, it was the death knell of a kingdom.

Mateso knelt on the cold marble floor, his dark robes pooling around him like a shadow. His head bowed low, though not in reverence. His triumph burned in his chest, but his eyes betrayed a hunger that even a crown could not satiate. Before him stood a Roman Catholic priest, his heavy robes gleaming in the torchlight, a gilded crown in his hands.

“In nomine Patris, et Filii, et Spiritus Sancti,” the priest intoned, his voice resonating through the grand hall as he raised the crown above Mateso’s head. “In the name of God, I crown you King of Africa.”

The golden circlet descended slowly, its weight pressing down not just on Mateso’s brow but on the very soul of the kingdom. The word Africa echoed through the hall like a curse. This was not the name of the united empire of Alkebulan It was the name given by outsiders, a mark of foreign rule and subjugation. The silence that followed was deafening, a hollow void filled with the unspoken grief of the people.

The crowd stood motionless, their faces masks of sorrow and quiet rage. Among them were nobles forced to attend, their heads bowed not in submission but in mourning. The air was thick with suppressed anger, a storm waiting to break. Yet no voice rose in defiance, for fear of the swords that lined the hall.

Outside, a boy tugged at his father’s sleeve, his whisper cutting through the heavy air. “He is not our king,” the boy said, his voice trembling with conviction. His father’s eyes flicked down to him, filled with fear and pride in equal measure. The man hushed him quickly, but the boy’s words lingered, a seed of rebellion sown in the hearts of all who heard.

When the ceremony was over and the nobles had gone, a tall foreigner in a coat of blue wool remained in the throne room. He was the envoy of the Western Trading Company, whose ships had carried the poison, the soldiers and the priest. He did not bow.

“The Company has kept its promise, Your Majesty,” he said, glancing at the crown. “Now you will keep yours. The ports of the coast are ours to trade from. And the Company will take its payment in the currency we agreed.”
Mateso did not look at him. “Take what you need from the villages,” he said. “The people have nothing else to give.”
The envoy smiled thinly and left. Behind him the doors closed, and the first chains of the Company were already being unloaded at the harbour.

Far from the palace, in the refuge of the Makua, a small fire flickered beneath the canopy of trees. Shida sat beside it, her arms wrapped protectively around Akachi. The child slept soundly, his tiny fists clutching the cloth that swaddled him. Each breath he took was a reminder of the fragile hope that still lived.
Elder Wekesa stood at the edge of the camp, his staff raised high toward the heavens. His voice was low, steady, yet it carried a power that resonated through the still night.
“The boy lives,” he said, his gaze fixed on the distant stars. “And the star shines still.”

The warriors and loyalists gathered around the fire, their faces etched with determination. They knew the weight of their task, the years of struggle that lay ahead. But in the soft glow of the firelight, the faintest glimmer of hope flickered.
The future of Alkebulan rested not in the hollow triumph of a usurper but in the small, sleeping child and the unyielding spirit of a kingdom that refused to die.

label: CHAPTER 3
title: Echoes of the Fallen Sun
p: The great hall of the Swahili Palace stood in haunting silence, its vastness consumed by shadows that flickered and swayed under the feeble glow of torches. Golden braziers, long extinguished, hung like relics of a forgotten age, their once-proud splendor now reduced to cold metal and cobwebs. The faint scent of stale incense clung to the air, a ghostly reminder of ceremonies that once filled the hall with life. Now, it resembled a tomb, a graveyard of dreams.

Mateso sat slumped on the Simbarashe throne, his figure a dark silhouette against the ivory backdrop. The throne, carved with intricate patterns of suns and birds, seemed to mock him with its grandeur. His fingers curled around the Simbarashe ring, its golden surface dull and lifeless in the wavering light. Once, it was said to channel the heavens, to connect kings to divine power and wisdom. But in his grasp, it felt cold, inert, and hollow.

He held it up to the light, turning it slowly. The faint gleam of gold caught his eye, its edges worn smooth by the hands of kings who had wielded it before him. Legends whispered of its power to bestow courage, wisdom, and the favor of the gods. Yet for Mateso, there was only silence. No whispers from the heavens. No answers. A bitter wind howled outside, rattling the stone walls of the palace and seeping into the hall. It carried the despair of a withering kingdom, the cries of starving children, and the mournful prayers of a broken people. Mateso clenched the ring tighter, his knuckles white against its metallic gleam. The people blamed him. The ministers judged him. Even the gods seemed to have abandoned him. His anger flared like a wildfire, burning away the seeds of doubt.
He slammed his fist against the throne’s armrest, the sharp crack echoing through the emptiness.

“They have failed me, not the other way around!” His voice lashed out, harsh and venomous, but the silence that followed felt like an accusation. The hall, with its vast emptiness, seemed to mock him. The ring lay heavy in his palm. He wanted to cast it aside, to shatter it and prove it held no power over him. But he couldn’t. He simply clutched it tighter, his breath ragged with frustration.

A faint knock broke the oppressive silence. The massive wooden door creaked open, and a servant stepped hesitantly into the room. His frame was small, almost swallowed by the weight of the hall’s grandeur. He bowed low, his trembling hands clutching the folds of his robe.

“My king...” The servant’s voice quivered, barely audible over the wind's mournful howl. “The ministers request your presence. The famine grows worse. Mateso’s lip curled in disdain. The mention of the ministers those scheming parasites only deepened the unease gnawing at him. His gaze fixed on the servant, sharp and unrelenting.
“They request?” Mateso’s words dripped with contempt, his voice a dagger aimed at the man’s heart. “And what would they have me do? Command the skies to rain?”

The servant flinched, his head bowing lower. He dared not speak. Mateso’s eyes narrowed, his fury barely restrained. He could feel the weight of their desperation, their silent accusations, like a thousand needles piercing his skin. “Tell them I will see them in the morning,” he muttered, dismissing the servant with a wave of his hand. “Now leave me.”
The servant hesitated for a moment, then bowed deeply and retreated, the massive doors creaking shut behind him.

Alone once more, Mateso sank deeper into the throne, his shoulders slumping under the invisible weight of his crown. The wind outside howled louder, its mournful cry seeping through the cracks and filling the hall with an eerie resonance. It was as if the very elements conspired against him, their whispers taunting his failures.

In the shadows, the flickering torchlight revealed the carvings of past kings etched into the walls, their eyes full of judgment. Their silent stares bore down on Mateso, and for a fleeting moment, he felt the crushing weight of their expectations.

The ring lay heavy in his palm, a cold reminder of the throne he had claimed but could not truly hold. The heavens remained silent, and the burden of his doubt grew heavier with each passing moment. In the dense, mist-covered forests far beyond the reach of the palace, the Makua gathered under the shroud of darkness. The air was heavy with the scent of damp earth and the faint tang of burning herbs. Shadows stretched and twisted beneath the dim moonlight, which barely pierced the canopy of ancient trees. The only illumination came from the crackling fire at the center of the circle, its flames casting fleeting patterns of light on the somber faces of the warriors and shamans.

Elder Wekesa sat cross-legged before the fire, his silhouette etched in stark relief against the orange glow. His weathered face bore the lines of years spent in service to the heavens, his eyes reflecting the weight of the burden he carried. In his hands rested his staff, its intricate carvings catching the flicker of the flames. Around him, the Makua knelt silently, their breaths shallow, their gazes fixed on their leader.

“The stars have dimmed,” Wekesa began, his voice a low murmur that seemed to blend with the crackle of the fire. Yet his words carried a solemn gravity, drawing every ear closer. “The boy’s star the light of God’s hand remains hidden. But the shadows stir.”

A faint rustle swept through the circle as the warriors shifted uneasily. The silence was broken by a broad-shouldered warrior leaning forward, his brow furrowed with doubt. His voice was rough, laced with a mixture of fear and defiance. “Elder, the land withers. Rivers dry. Crops fail. The people cry out. Can the boy still save us?”

Wekesa’s gaze hardened, the firelight casting sharp shadows across his face. He tightened his grip on the staff, his voice cutting through the tension like a blade. “He must,” he declared, his tone leaving no room for argument. “The ring has been placed in the wrong hands, and its anger is upon us. The usurper king has doomed us all.”

The words hung heavy in the air, their weight pressing upon the gathered warriors. Wekesa turned his gaze eastward, toward the distant silhouette of the palace barely visible beyond the horizon. The firelight dimmed for a moment, as if mirroring the despair that clung to the gathering.

“But I have seen it,” Wekesa continued, his voice softening, yet resonating with an unshakable certainty. “The Simbarashe ring will return to its chosen. The stars do not lie. They whisper of the boy’s survival. They speak of his rise.”

For a long moment Wekesa said nothing. The fire hissed. When he spoke again, his voice had changed. It was no longer the voice of a leader giving orders, but of an old man carrying a secret that had grown too heavy to carry alone.

“You know the Simbarashe ring as the crown of the heavens’ favour,” he said. “But the elders of my elders knew it as something more. When the first king united the kingdoms of Alkebulan, he did not do it alone. The fire-queen of Brava Island stood beside him. Nyai Roro. She gave her strength to his wars, and he swore before the heavens that she would share his throne.”
A ripple of unease ran through the circle. Some of the younger warriors made the sign against evil at the sound of her name.

“But when the land was won,” Wekesa went on, “the first king looked at her power and was afraid. He broke his oath. With the light of the ring he bound her beneath the Fire Pit, and there she has burned for a thousand years.” He lifted his eyes to the warriors, one by one. “Since that night, every true king has carried the ring, and every true king has held the seal. The ring answers only to the blood of the first king. But the seal holds for as long as the ring is honoured. If a king should ever cast it away…”
He did not finish. He did not need to.
“Mateso would never throw away the very thing that makes him king,” the young warrior said, though his voice lacked conviction.

“A man who cannot hear the heavens will one day curse them,” Wekesa replied. “I have seen it in the fire. A night when gold falls from the Ivory Tower like a dying star. On that night, the queen of the pit will wake.”

He turned to a lean boy at the edge of the circle, barely old enough to carry a spear. “Jengo. From tonight, you will watch the tower. Every night, for as long as it takes. When the gold falls, you will bring it to me before any other hand can touch it.”
The boy swallowed hard and bowed his head. “I will watch, Elder.”

A shaman seated near Wekesa raised his head, his face painted with intricate patterns of protection and foresight. “And what of the curse?” he asked, his voice barely audible. “The land is bleeding, Elder. The rivers run dry, and the crops wither. The people grow restless. They say the ring” he hesitated, his voice faltering, “rejects its bearer.”

Murmurs rippled through the circle, a chorus of fear and unease. Wekesa’s expression grew darker, his grip on his staff tightening as he stood. The movement silenced the murmurs, his voice steady as he spoke.

“The curse will spread as long as the wrong hands hold the ring,” he said, his tone resolute. “It rejects the usurper, as it should. The heavens will not bless his rule. But the boy’s time will come. We must guard him until it does.”

One warrior, younger than the rest, rose abruptly, his hand resting on the hilt of his blade. “And if it doesn’t? What if the boy cannot save us?” His voice was sharp, cutting through the reverence of the gathering. “What if the heavens have abandoned us, Elder?”
Wekesa turned to face him, his expression a blend of sorrow and conviction. “The heavens do not abandon the righteous,” he said firmly. “But they test us. The curse is not our end it is our trial.”
The young warrior hesitated, his defiance wavering under the elder’s unyielding gaze. Slowly, he lowered himself back to the ground, his hand falling from his blade.

The tension in the circle remained thick as Wekesa raised his staff high, its carved patterns gleaming in the firelight. His voice rose, steady and commanding. “The Simbarashe ring will choose again. The boy’s star will rise, and with it, the light of Alkebulan will shine once more. But we must endure.”

The warriors and shamans bowed their heads, their faces reflecting a mixture of hope and despair. The fire crackled louder, sending sparks into the night sky, as if carrying their prayers to the stars.

In the silence that followed, the distant cries of nocturnal creatures filled the air. The forest seemed to close in around them, a reminder of the fragile refuge they held. But as Wekesa lowered his staff and gazed eastward once more, his eyes burned with the fire of conviction.
“The boy lives,” he whispered, more to himself than to the circle. “And the ring will not remain silent forever.”
One year became two. Two became ten. The rains that should have come each season gathered on the horizon, darkened the sky with promise, and then drifted away without shedding a single drop.

Mateso grew older on the Simbarashe throne. The proud black of his beard turned to iron grey. He slept little and trusted less. Ministers who questioned him disappeared in the night, and their seats in the council were filled by men who had learned to say only yes. The foreign traders who had crowned him grew richer with every year. Their ships, which had once carried silk and spices, now left the coast with a different cargo: men, women and children in chains, taken from the hungry villages in payment for the king’s debts. Their caravans carried the king’s seal, and no one dared to stop them.

And every night, in the shadow of the palace walls, Jengo watched the Ivory Tower. He watched it through eighteen rainy seasons that brought no rain. He watched it as his boyish frame grew into the body of a warrior, as his friends married and his mother grew old. Some among the Makua laughed at him. The old man’s dream, they called his watch. Jengo did not laugh. He watched.
Somewhere far away, on a coast where fishermen pulled empty nets from a tired sea, a boy grew into a young man, never knowing whose blood ran in his veins.
Eighteen years passed. And the suffering of the Great Swahili Nation deepened.

The once-vibrant fields in the villages lay cracked and barren, their rich soil reduced to lifeless dust. Crops withered overnight, their green stalks curling into brittle husks as if cursed by unseen hands.
Men dug deep into the earth, their fingers raw and bleeding as they searched for water in empty wells. Even the rivers, once lifelines to the people, had shrunk to shallow, stagnant pools.

In the cities, the air buzzed with tension. Market squares that once overflowed with laughter and trade now echoed with cries of despair. Merchants stood behind stalls stocked with empty sacks, their voices hoarse from desperate haggling. Women wailed openly, clutching their starving children close, their hollow eyes searching for salvation that never came.
“Where is the king?” the people shouted, their voices rising in desperation. “Where is the rain?

The cries of the people grew louder with each passing day, their voices carried by the dry winds to the palace gates. But within the stone walls, Mateso remained distant, the weight of the nation’s suffering pressing down upon him. Rumors of rebellion seeped into the air like smoke, whispered by servants and echoed in the dim halls. The ministers, their faces pale and drawn, dared to confront their king.
One by one, they filed into the throne room, their robes heavy with the scent of sweat and fear. The room was oppressively silent, the golden braziers casting flickering shadows on the stone walls.

Mateso, grey now and hollow-eyed after eighteen years of drought, sat rigid on the Simbarashe throne, his fingers drumming on the armrest. The faint glow of the ring on his finger barely pierced the dim light, its once-mighty power seemingly extinguished.
“The land is dying, Your Majesty,” one minister began, his voice trembling as he stepped forward. “The people are starving. If we do not act, there will be no kingdom left to rule.”

A murmur of agreement rippled through the group, though none dared to meet Mateso’s piercing gaze. The king rose abruptly, his movements sharp and commanding silence. His dark eyes scanned the gathered ministers, his expression a volatile mix of fury and frustration.

“Act?” he repeated, his voice cold and biting. He lifted the Simbarashe ring, its golden surface catching the dim light. “You come to me with demands, yet this “he thrust the ring forward “is the cause of our suffering!”
His voice rose, anger sharpening his words. “The shamans promised power. They spoke of destiny. And yet, look at the land! Look at my kingdom! The ring has cursed us!”

Mateso flung his arm wide, the gesture as wild as his tone. The ministers exchanged uneasy glances, their fear thick in the air. One of them, an older man with deep-set eyes and trembling hands, hesitated before stepping forward.
“Perhaps... perhaps the shamans were right,” he said cautiously, his voice barely above a whisper. “The ring rejects you, my king.”

The words struck like a hammer, echoing in the silence. Mateso’s face darkened, his lips curling into a snarl. He descended the steps of the throne, his fury radiating like heat. The ministers shrank back, their bodies tense with fear.
“Get out,” Mateso growled, his voice low and dangerous. The fire in his eyes burned brighter as he repeated, louder this time, “Out!”

The ministers scrambled to obey, their movements clumsy in their haste to leave the room. The heavy doors creaked shut behind them, sealing Mateso in the oppressive silence of the throne room. He stood alone, the faint glow of the ring casting long shadows on the cold stone walls.

His hands clenched into fists, his breathing heavy as he stared at the Simbarashe ring. For a fleeting moment, doubt flickered across his face. What if the ministers were right? What if the shamans’ prophecies had spoken the truth all along?
But pride quickly smothered the thought. “Fools,” he muttered, his voice echoing in the emptiness. “They know nothing.”

Outside, the faint cries of the people reached the palace, a haunting reminder of the kingdom’s suffering. But Mateso turned his back to the sound, retreating to the shadows of the throne, his heart a tempest of rage and denial.

The Ivory Tower loomed high above the sleeping capital, its spire piercing the night sky like a defiant spear. The wind howled around it, a mournful dirge carrying the weight of a kingdom in decline. Mateso climbed the worn stone steps, his movements erratic, and his breaths shallow and ragged. Each step echoed in the hollow silence, a rhythm of madness that drove him higher.

The chill of the night air seeped into his bones, but he barely noticed. His mind was a flame with anger and despair, the walls of his thoughts closing in on him. His cloak whipped around him, a dark shroud that seemed to mirror the storm brewing within.

At the summit, the city sprawled before him, veiled in the dim glow of a crescent moon. Once a jewel of the Great Swahili Nation, the capital now lay in oppressive silence. Fires in the hearts of homes had long since burned out, their smoke curling faintly into the night air. The streets were barren, lifeless as if the very spirit of the city had been snuffed out.

In his hand, Mateso gripped the Simbarashe ring. The once-lustrous gold felt cold and heavy, its intricate carvings dull under the pale light. He turned it over in his fingers, his eyes narrowing as he studied it.
“This relic,” he muttered his voice raw and trembling. “It has brought nothing but ruin.”
The words came unbidden, spilling forth like poison. “It cursed my father,” he continued, his tone rising. “It cursed my brother. And now... it curses me.”

The wind howled louder, as if to drown his words, but Mateso’s fury only grew. He stepped to the edge of the tower, his gaze fixed on the city below. The sprawling streets and distant horizon felt insignificant, unworthy of his rage.
“I am king!” he shouted, his voice a raw echo carried on the wind. “I have no need of you! If this is your will, then take it back!”

With one final, desperate cry, Mateso hurled the Simbarashe ring into the night. The golden band gleamed briefly before vanishing into the dark abyss. For a moment, all was still. Silence hung heavy in the air, broken only by the sound of the wind rushing past the tower. Then, the earth began to tremble.

A low, guttural rumble rose from the depths of the ground, growing louder and more violent with each passing second. The palace shuddered, its ancient foundations groaning in protest. Dust rained from the ceilings, and distant walls cracked under the strain. The tremor spread outward, rippling through the land like a shockwave.

In the forests beyond the city, animals scattered in frantic flight, their cries piercing the stillness of the night. Rivers froze, their once-constant flow halting as if in awe of the moment. The air grew thick and heavy, suffocating in its unnatural weight.

Above, the stars flickered. The constellations, the eternal watchers of Alkebulan, dimmed one by one, their light faltering as if mourning the land’s fate. A veil of darkness seemed to spread across the heavens, obscuring the divine witnesses.

Mateso staggered back from the edge of the tower, his breath coming in sharp, ragged gasps. For the first time, doubt pierced the armor of his arrogance. His hands trembled as he gripped the stone ledge, his gaze locked on the dark horizon.
“What have I done?” he whispered, the words barely audible over the wind.

The tremors subsided, leaving an eerie stillness in their wake. But the silence was not a relief it was a warning. Something had shifted. The land, the heavens, and the balance of power had all been disturbed. And in the cold light of the fading stars, Mateso stood alone, the weight of his actions pressing down on him like an iron shroud.
Far below, the capital remained silent. But in the hearts of the people, a new fear took root a fear that their king, their supposed savior, had unleashed something far worse than famine or drought.
And for the first time, even Mateso began to believe it.
Far below, crouched among the dry reeds of the empty palace moat, Jengo had seen it fall.
A thread of gold, tumbling through the dark like a dying star. Exactly as the old man had said.

For eighteen years he had imagined this moment, and now that it had come, his body moved before his mind could catch up. He scrambled down the cracked bank, his bare feet sliding on dust that had once been mud. The ring lay half-buried in the dead earth, its stone glowing faintly, as though breathing. When his fingers closed around it, it was warm. Not the warmth of the sun, but the warmth of a living thing.
He did not look back at the tower. He ran.

He ran through the silent streets of the capital and out through a gap in the broken wall. He ran through the night, through the forest, until his lungs burned and his legs shook. When he finally stumbled into the Makua camp, Elder Wekesa was already standing by the fire, as if he had been waiting.
Jengo opened his hand. The ring glowed between them.
Wekesa did not take it at once. He looked at it for a long time, and the firelight showed the tears in his old eyes. “So,” he whispered. “It begins.”

He wrapped the ring in a strip of white cloth marked with sacred signs and tucked it inside his robe, close to his heart. “No hand but one will ever wear this again,” he said. “And that hand is still out there, somewhere in the dark.”

Far to the west, on the cursed Brava Island, the ground trembled as the Fire Pit dormant for centuries erupted with violent fury. The earth split open, vomiting plumes of ash and fire into the starless sky. Lava oozed forth like molten blood, carving fiery veins into the jagged terrain. A deafening roar split the night, as if the island itself was screaming.

The air grew heavy with sulfur, burning the throats of villagers along the coast. They stirred from uneasy sleep, drawn outside by the red glow that painted the horizon. The sea boiled, hissing and steaming, its surface reflecting the chaos above. Shadows writhed and stretched across the land, twisting unnaturally as though the light of the fire had given them life. Legends of the Fire Pit, whispered in fear by the elders, came rushing back to their minds.

“The goddess of the pit!” an old woman wailed, clutching her chest as she collapsed to her knees. “She rises to consume us!” The villagers scattered, their desperate cries lost beneath the roar of the flames. Legends long whispered in fear were now a living reality, and no one dared to look back.

A voice rose from the depths of the Fire Pit, a sound that was both a whisper and a scream, soft as silk yet sharp as the edge of a blade. It carried on the wind, slipping into the ears of those who dared to listen.
“I have waited... and now I rise.”

The villagers froze, their faces pale with terror. Some fell to their knees, muttering prayers to forgotten gods. Others fled, their bare feet pounding against the scorched earth as they disappeared into the darkness. But none could escape the pull of the Fire Pit. The ground heaved, and from its fiery heart, Nyai Roro emerged.
Her arrival was heralded by a wave of oppressive heat, a pulse that seemed to bend the very air around her. Her form was otherworldly dark, ethereal figure crowned with an unholy light.

Her face, carved with divine beauty, burned with the intensity of twin suns. Her eyes, molten orbs of fire, swept over the land with a gaze that pierced the soul. Her very breath carried the heat of a furnace, scorching the air around her.

Her body shimmered and shifted a surreal blend of power and elegance. The lower half of her body was that of a lion, its golden fur streaked with black, muscles rippling as she moved with predatory grace. Her back was crowned with vast, black wings that unfurled like a storm, their edges sparking with embers. Each step she took left smoldering prints in the earth, as if the land itself bowed to her presence. The ground beneath her feet quaked, sending tremors that resonated across the island.
“Awaken, my children,” Nyai Roro whispered her voice a melody that carried both allure and malice. It was a sound that stirred the depths of fear and fascination, impossible to resist.

The Fire Pit bubbled violently, and from its core, dark figures began to emerge. Twisted warriors of shadow and flame clawed their way into the light, their forms grotesque and shifting. Some bore the appearance of men, but their faces were masks of anguish, their limbs elongated and distorted. Others were hulking beasts, their bodies covered in jagged armor that seemed to grow from their flesh.

Their eyes glowed with the same infernal fire that radiated from Nyai Roro, and as they stood before her, they moved in perfect, unsettling silence. The twisted beings fell to one knee before their mistress, their molten eyes blazing with reverence. Their grotesque forms trembled with eagerness, their claws raking the earth as they awaited her command.

Nyai Roro raised her wings high, her silhouette towering against the fiery backdrop. For a moment she simply breathed, drinking in the open sky she had not seen in a thousand years. Then her gaze turned east, toward the lands of Alkebulan, and her face hardened.

“I gave him my fire,” she said softly, and the island seemed to listen. “I burned his enemies and raised his walls. He swore that I would sit beside him on that throne. And when the land was his, he chained me in the pit like a beast.” Her claws sank into the burning earth. “A thousand years, my children. A thousand years of fire, while his sons wore my prison on their fingers and called it the favour of the heavens.”
She lifted her head, as though catching a scent on the wind. Far to the east, faint and flickering, a single star struggled to shine. Her lips curled into a cruel smile.

“His blood still walks this land. I can feel it.” She spread her wings wide. “Find me the child of the star. And then we march on the house of the oath-breaker. The age of men ends tonight. The world shall kneel before me, and the king who sits on the Simbarashe throne shall tremble.”
The warriors roared, their cries a chilling blend of agony and triumph. As one, they began their march, their twisted forms disappearing into the shadows as they spread across the land.
Behind them, the Fire Pit pulsed with malevolent energy, a reminder that Brava Island had become the birthplace of destruction.
Above, the stars remained dim, their light no match for the rising tide of darkness.

Back in the palace, Mateso awoke with a start. The chamber trembled, the stones groaning under an unseen pressure. The air was thick with a sense of impending doom, carrying the weight of an ancient power that had been stirred from its slumber.
“Your Majesty!” A guard burst in, his face pale with terror. His armor clinked as he stumbled forward, his chest heaving. “The people there are screams in the streets! The ground shakes!”

Mateso pushed himself up, his heart pounding like a war drum in his chest. The tremor beneath his feet seemed to echo the turmoil within him. “What madness is this?” he demanded his voice sharp with authority. But deep down, he already knew the answer. The earth had shifted, and with it, something far greater and more terrible had awakened.

He moved to the window, his hands gripping the stone sill as he looked out over the city. Fires flickered faintly in the distance, their light swallowed by the darkness that seemed to press down from the sky. The streets below writhed with panic. Shadows darted between the alleys, and the anguished cries of the people rose like a mournful chorus.

As Mateso strained to listen, a voice carried on the wind. It began as a faint murmur, like a melody whispered from a distant realm. The sound seemed to wrap around him, slipping into his ears and curling in his chest like a cold hand. “The queen of the pit has risen.”
The words hung in the air like a death sentence, each syllable soaked in malice. The voice resonated with an otherworldly power, leaving no doubt of its source.

Mateso staggered back, his breath catching in his throat. His hands shook as he clenched them into fists, trying to suppress the wave of dread that threatened to engulf him. For the first time since he had claimed the throne, he felt the icy grip of true fear.

The chamber trembled again, the stones groaning louder. Mateso’s gaze darted back to the guard, whose terror mirrored the chaos outside. “Seal the palace,” he ordered, his voice unsteady but firm. “No one enters. No one leaves.”
The guard hesitated for a moment, then nodded and disappeared into the shadows, his hurried footsteps echoing through the corridors.

Left alone, Mateso turned his attention back to the ring on his finger the Simbarashe ring, now cold and unresponsive. He lifted it to the faint light of the torches, his eyes narrowing as a tremor ran through him. Was this its doing? Had it called forth the queen of the pit? Or had he doomed himself and the kingdom by casting aside its power?
His mind spiraled with questions, but no answers came. Only the haunting voice on the wind, repeating its chilling refrain:
“The queen of the pit has risen.”
